extracted.intended_audience: scientists and engineers who interact with journalists (researchers, graduate students, science communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scientists on preparing for and conducting interviews with journalists, building media relationships, and tailoring messages so research reaches the public and decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of working with journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: How can the news media help you reach your communication and engagement goals? Working with journalists gives scientists opportunities to provide accurate, informative updates about the latest research to the general public, decision-makers, funders, and other scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific benefits listed: Reach a wider audience (beyond active information seekers), Raise awareness (increase public awareness of specific work and of science in general), Create positive attitudes (stories can generate enthusiasm for research and support for funding). Use these goals to frame whether and how to engage with media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the audience (and their audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before giving an interview, consider both the direct audience – the journalist – and the intended audience – their readers, viewers, or listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the journalist about their audiences and tailor core messages to those audiences. Public affairs officers can help tailor messages to specific audiences. Understanding both layers improves odds of successfully reaching the public you care about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the journalist’s role and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct Audience: The Journalist — Before interacting with a journalist, it’s helpful to understand how and why they do their job the way they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists: consult sources; aim for accuracy; weigh evidence and use the most relevant tidbits in the story; must meet their editor’s or producer’s demands; write in a unique style and are not required to share stories before publication; write/produce quickly (some produce >5 stories/day); inform (not educate) the public and may not provide lengthy background. Expect fast turnarounds and editorial changes that don’t necessarily indicate inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare core three-point message
rubrics_metrics.description: What is my core three-point message on this topic and why should the audience care?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan core messages in advance no matter the interview length. Articulate a concise, three-point message. Also be prepared to answer: (1) what is new, and (2) why should readers be interested? Short, well-organized messages increase clarity and fit journalists' time constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate difficult or controversial questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to anticipate difficult or potentially controversial questions (and your responses) before the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare answers for likely critical or sensitive angles so you can respond promptly and stay on-message. This reduces risk of being surprised on short deadlines and helps maintain accuracy and composure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be punctual and ready to meet deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists want their sources to provide credible, accurate information in time to meet their deadlines, which could be a few minutes or a few hours after your conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make every effort to be on time for interviews, have core messages ready, and be reachable within reporters' timelines. Delays or unavailability can result in missed opportunities or incomplete reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messages to the journalist’s audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate goal when talking to a journalist is to convey your core messages to their readers, viewers, or listeners; tailor your core messages to those audiences to improve the odds of successfully reaching them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask journalists about audience values, interests, and concerns. Use institutional public information officers for advice on tailoring messages. Different outlets and formats (TV, radio, print, web) require different framing and levels of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a media network (PIOs, scientist-communicators, journalists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a network of resources to make navigating the news media more efficient — and enjoyable!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get to know public information officers (PIOs) at universities, government agencies, and organizations; other scientists who have media experience; and local journalists. Use PIOs for introductions, share best practices with experienced peers, start a blog, comment on public websites, and attend media-friendly conferences to become a known resource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public information officers (PIOs) and platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Public information officers act as liaisons between scientists and journalists and can provide assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many PIOs have journalism or science backgrounds and can help prepare materials, make introductions, and advise on messaging. Most PIO contact information is online; EurekAlert! Science Sources is suggested for finding PIO contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Become a science journalist or gain newsroom experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn what it’s like from the inside by applying to fellowship or internship programs to work in newsrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AAAS Mass Media Science and Engineering Fellows place scientists in newsrooms to work as print, web, radio, or TV journalists. Applicants should be students or recent graduates in science/engineering fields. Hands-on experience helps scientists understand newsroom pace, editorial styles, and how journalists select and shape stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a proactive resource to journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase the chances of being contacted by journalists by being a readily available resource in your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include becoming a go-to local expert, starting a personal blog, commenting on public websites, attending media-friendly conferences, and cultivating relationships so journalists think of you when they need expertise.
